I’ve been running my restaurant for twelve years—long hours, but it used to feel rewarding. Lately, though, I can’t enjoy anything. Not the compliments from customers, not even time with my husband. It’s like a numbness settled inside, and I don’t feel joy anymore. Ever since that night—the break-in, when they came behind the counter—I get jumpy anytime a door slams or someone shouts. I flinch hard, sometimes drop whatever I’m holding.  

I keep thinking it should’ve been me who called the police sooner. Maybe if I had… I don’t know. I can’t stop replaying it. And I'm just so angry now—constant, simmering—even at people who don’t deserve it.  

Focusing is hard. During meetings with suppliers, my mind drifts. I hear things too—voices calling my name when no one’s there, once even in the walk-in cooler. I can’t tell if it’s stress or… something else. They don’t feel like flashbacks, just random, but I don’t know. I’m scared to say too much, like you’ll think I’m losing my mind. But I had to come. I can’t run the place like this.
D018-D005_h001.question_a:
I’ve been struggling ever since that night during the armed robbery at my restaurant—three months ago now. I still hear the gunshots in my head, like they’re right there. If a car backfires or a plate drops, I jump—sometimes I drop things, my heart races, I can’t breathe. It’s like I’m back in that moment. I keep seeing the gunman’s face, even when my eyes are open. It’s not like I’m losing touch, but it feels so real—it’s part of what happened. These aren’t random voices or strange thoughts; it’s always *that* night.  

I love my husband, but I don’t feel it the way I used to. I can’t enjoy anything—the café, our dinners, nothing. I feel numb most of the time. And guilty. I keep thinking I should’ve stayed calm, should’ve done something differently. I get angry—at myself, at the world—like there’s a fire inside I can’t put out.  

Focusing on orders, staff schedules, even conversations—it’s hard. My mind’s always scanning, waiting for danger. But aside from reliving the trauma, I’m not hearing voices telling me things, and I know I’m not being watched for reasons beyond that night. This isn’t psychosis—it’s the aftermath of something real.
D018-D005_h001.question_b:
I’ve been running my restaurant for twelve years, and up until six months ago, I could handle the stress—long hours, managing staff, keeping my husband happy. But lately, little things set me off. A car backfiring outside sent me to the floor last week, trembling. I can’t focus during dinner rush anymore—orders get mixed up because I lose track mid-sentence. 

I don’t feel joy anymore. Not with my husband, not with anything. I’m angry all the time, like there’s a fire under my skin. I keep thinking it was my fault—what happened during that armed robbery last year. I didn’t fight back. I froze. Now I punish myself every day for it.

But what’s worse—what I can’t explain—is the voices. They come out of nowhere, not tied to the robbery. One hisses insults about me being worthless, another argues with me when I’m alone in the kitchen. They don’t replay the trauma—they attack me, accuse me, tell me people are watching. I know it sounds crazy, but they’re not echoes of that night. They’re separate. And they’ve been getting louder.

D018-D005_h013.question_both:
I’ve been having a hard time lately—just over the past few months, really. Ever since that incident last year when I was showing a property and things… got out of hand. I don’t like to talk about it, but sometimes even hearing a loud noise, like a door slamming in an empty house, makes my chest tighten and my hands shake. I avoid those kinds of listings now—older homes, quiet neighborhoods. I tell myself it’s just business, but honestly, I can’t stand being alone in a room that feels too still.  

I keep thinking it was my fault. I should’ve left earlier, should’ve brought someone with me. Now I feel like the world isn’t safe anymore—like danger’s always waiting in the shadows. I snap sometimes, too. Last week I threw my phone across the office after a client raised their voice. It scared me more than them.  

And there are times—usually when I’m exhausted—I swear I hear footsteps behind me, or someone whispering my name in an empty room. I turn around, and no one’s there. It’s not like seeing something, exactly. Just… sounds. I don’t know if it’s stress, grief, or something worse. I can’t tell what’s real anymore.
D018-D005_h013.question_a:
I’ve been struggling for over a year now since... well, since what happened during that open house. I was alone in the property when someone broke in. I managed to hide, but I heard everything—his voice, the footsteps, the crash when he threw something. Ever since, any loud noise—even a door slamming in an empty house—sends my heart racing, and I can’t breathe right. Sometimes I even feel the same sweat on my palms, like I’m back there.

I don’t talk about it. I avoid thinking about it, but the memories just come—especially at night. I blame myself. I should’ve left earlier. Should’ve locked the doors. I keep thinking the world isn’t safe—nowhere is. I used to love showing homes, but now I see danger in every corner.

Sometimes, I hear that same voice—muttering the words he said. It’s like he’s right there. But I know it’s not real. It’s always *that* voice, *that* moment—never anything else. I haven’t seen monsters or strangers following me. It’s just him, just that night. And when the stress builds, I’ve thrown things—once shattered a lamp. I don’t know how to calm down anymore.
D018-D005_h013.question_b:
I’ve been struggling for years, ever since my divorce turned really messy—there was physical danger, things I don’t like to talk about. Even now, just a tone of voice or someone standing too close can make my chest tighten and my hands shake, like I’m right back there. I try not to think about it—I avoid old neighborhoods, certain conversations—but it still creeps in. I’ve started believing the world is just full of people waiting to hurt you. I blame myself sometimes, like I should’ve left sooner or handled things differently.

Lately, though, things have changed. I hear voices—clear as yours—commenting on what I’m doing, even when no one’s around. They aren’t talking about the trauma. They call me “weak” or argue about random things, like whether I should take a listing. It’s not flashbacks—it’s like strangers in my head. I’ve yelled at them, thrown a tablet once when the voices got loud. My assistant noticed and was scared. This isn’t just reacting to the past. These thoughts feel outside me, and they’ve been getting harder to ignore for over a year now.
